blocks.value: This is the most important thing in the lesson.

items: **`==`** compares the **references**: whether two variables point to the same object in memory.

blocks.value:
str1 == str2          // true, same memory location, same content
str1 == str3          // false, different memory locations
str1.equals(str3)     // true, same contents
str3 == str4          // false, different memory locations
str3.equals(str4)     // true, same contents

Read that list twice. `str1`, `str3`, and `str4` all contain the word `Computer`, yet `==` says two of them are different. Because both literals produce the same shared object, `str1 == str2` is `true`, which is exactly what makes this bug so dangerous. **Your test with literals passes, and the program fails the moment the string comes from user input or a file.**
**Rule: use `equals()` for strings, every time.** Reserve `==` for primitives.
